This course will survey American literature from its beginnings to
the middle of the nineteenth century. We will consider the voices of men and
women, the enslaved and the free, and the colonized and the colonizer. Through
first-hand accounts, journals, lectures, novels, and poetry, we will explore
how early Americans viewed and responded to the various events of their day,
and understand how these texts reflect historical, cultural, and literary
moments in American history.
This
survey of American Literature will examine the most influential and significant
writings of the United States, which were produced between the 15th century and
the Civil War. The course is organized thematically, rather than
chronologically. As such the texts we will read present the emergence of both a
nation and its identity.
This
survey course is designed to introduce you to a wide and rich variety of
American literature from its colonial beginnings to the mid-19th century,
including works representing some of the diverse ethnic and racial
strands of our literary heritage as well as texts by women
writers frequently excluded from literary
collections. Since this course covers writings from the colonial
period through the Civil War, we will become familiar with the historical and
cultural circumstances surrounding the production of a given text and explore
the development and expression of some fundamental ideas—-assumptions, myths,
and beliefs—that still influence the ways Americans think about themselves and
their society today. In addition to studying a range of prose, poetry,
and fictional works, we will also closely examine their aesthetic or rhetorical
dimensions and practice ways of identifying representative issues and
themes. The course uses You Tube and other media
as part of its instruction.

AML 3031 is a literary history course, focusing on broader literary movements in indigenous and British colonial America and what is now the U.S. Literature from this period uses genres and language that are less familiar to modern readers. Early American readers and publishers were suspicious of fiction and wanted “truth and beauty” instead (moral lessons and poetic forms). Poetry was an esteemed formal genre. Sermon, history, poetry, polemic, travel narrative, personal narrative, and origin story proliferated during this time.
This course covers three literary historical periods:
1) indigenous, early settlement and colonial literature;
2) the Enlightenment or “Age of Reason”; and
3) the 19th-century American “Renaissance” and “Age of Reform.”

The course addresses how specific literary texts produced during these historical periods confront questions which constitute and underpin American culture and history. Thematic focus uses origin stories.
Assignments: Weekly readings and quizzes; bi-weekly essay postings; revision of one bi-weekly essay, final exam.

AMERICAN POETRY.
The purpose of this course is to
read, discuss, and analyze poems written in America during the twentieth
century, focusing especially on formal components of poetry in relation to
social conditions. The preeminent scholar Helen Vendler once remarked, “Twentieth-century
American poetry has been one of the glories of modern literature.” Indeed, the
twentieth century in America saw the great poems of Robert Frost, Marianne
Moore, Langston Hughes, Robert Hayden, Gwendolyn Brooks, Elizabeth Bishop,
Sylvia Plath, Allen Ginsberg, Adrienne Rich, Sharon Olds, Lucille Clifton, Joy
Harjo, and many more. These poets, and so many others, offer something of an
emotional and intellectual record of a tumultuous century that redefined the
country and the world. We will identify the connections between the great
innovations of modernism and the so-called postmodern endeavors of
confessionalism, Black Arts poetry, the Beat Generation, the New York school,
and the Black Mountain poets. We will consider our time period to be the “long
twentieth century,” beginning with the proto-modern poems of Walt Whitman,
Emily Dickinson, and Paul Laurence Dunbar and ending in our present moment with
21st-century poems.

Topic: American Dramas.
A nation defines itself on its stage, and so we will
read plays from the past one hundred years and consider how each one represents
America. This class requires active engagement beyond weekly discussions.
Students will perform scenes collaboratively online, record monologues, and
design visual images as part of their dramatic interpretations. Playwrights
include August Wilson, Tony Kushner, David Henry Hwang, Donald Margulies,
Quiara Alegria Hudes, Lynne Nottage, Larissa FastHorse. This class is fully online.

"Political Literature in the 19th Century".
This semester-long webcourse examines political literature in
the long nineteenth century, beginning with antebellum abolitionist texts and
ending with representations of urban conditions at the beginning of the 20th
century. Students will investigate how each text responds to their contemporary
political landscape, socio- and geopolitical upheavals, and a shifting
understanding of the role of the Federal government. Finally, students
will consider how and why these texts continue to be relevant today.

will examine literatures written about the American South from the Antebellum
period through modern-day. We will consider authors such as Kate Chopin, Zora
Neale Hurston, William Faulkner, and Flannery O’Connor, among others. We will
consider key movements in Southern literature and the ways in which each author
defines “Southerness” and the American South’s storied but haunted history.

Until the 1980s,
anthologies of American literature included only Bradstreet and Emily Dickinson
as American women authors before 1900. However, many colonial American women
wrote and were published, sometimes in genres that are less familiar to us now.
We will study poems, letters, petitions, epitaphs, speeches, sampler verses,
broadsides, journals, diaries, commonplace books, household manuals,
travelogues, captivity narratives, and more by early modern women living in
colonial America and the newly formed U.S.
Required tasks: Heavy reading, weekly quizzes, midterm, final
project, bi-weekly essays, one of which will be revised into a formal essay for
a grade.

The goal of this course is to attempt
to answer certain questions raised by the African-American presence in American
life through its literature. By addressing issues of identity and ethnicity; in
other words, looking at the implications of what it means to be “African
American” as explored through literature, we will try to unravel and situate
the larger construct within literary modernity, of the relationship between
race and art in a meaningful way. In other words, this course will raise such
important questions as, how does the African-American or Black artist negotiate
what Du Bois once theorized and concluded to be the “strangeness of being black
in America?” What is “the Blackness of Blackness?” and of course, how does
African-American literature negotiate that complicated but foundational thesis
of the Du Boisian, “double consciousness,” in its relationship with a general
American reality, a well indeed as the Black Atlantic? At the end of this
semester we may come to some understanding of the aesthetic as well as
historical, and even political dimensions of African-American literature by
examining how African American writers have used different artistic and
narrative techniques to raise questions, explore, and even expand the
relationship between history and art.

This
class will survey literature by Puerto Rican writers both on the island and on
the mainland starting with authors seeking freedom from Spanish Colonial rule
followed by those writing against American political and cultural domination,
to the “Bootstraps” generation, through the Nuyorican poets, and up to
contemporary spoken word artists. This
class seeks to provide a general interdisciplinary survey of Puerto Rican
cultural production including a variety of genre such as poetry,
fiction, non-fiction (including speeches and newspaper columns), drama, and
film. Using a chronological procedure and contextual process, we will explore
the socio-political and economic factors leading to Puerto Rican migration to
the mainland with a particular focus on Puerto Ricans in Central Florida.

In contrast to the often romantic
depiction of the American Indian in history or films, this course surveys
Native American literature from its traditional origins—including tales, songs,
and oratory—to more modern responses in autobiography, fiction, poetry, and
other contemporary genres by writers such as N. Scott Momaday and Louise
Erdrich. In addition to learning about an alternate, indigenous history and culture of
North America and the “oral tradition” in different periods and regions, this
course aims to explore a series of thematic and aesthetic continuities and to
understand the various issues that Native Americans face both on and off
reservation communities today. This course uses You Tube and other media as
part of its instruction. Course requirements include reading, discussion posts,
brief written responses, a course paper, and a final exam.

American literature since 1970. Our historical focus starts with the so-called
“second wave” of Native American nonfiction, novels, poetry, and short fiction.
We will read six books by Native American authors and consider how these works
express a range of perspectives on contemporary Native American presence and
history; relationship to land; and representations and cultural
survivance. Required tasks: Two short papers; midterm; final; bi-weekly

AML 4300 (RI) is an asynchronous online course focused on the works of acclaimed contemporary Chickasaw writer and ecofeminist Linda Hogan. We will read Hogan’s poetry, essays, memoir, and three of her novels.

This course has a Research Intensive designation that will appear on your UCF transcript. This designation is one of UCF’s four High Impact practices and challenges students to engage actively in research processes underlying professional work in the discipline of literary studies. 30% of the final grade is based on the final research paper you will submit; 20% of the course grade is based on the successful completion of stepped research assignments; 5% of the course grade is based on a final poster presentation about your research project. Each step of this research process will be completed in scaffolded assignments that require students to produce documents used in literary research. Three 750-word essays; weekly quizzes; one conference length (10-12 page; 2500-word) essay with research; heavy reading load.

Applies toward English major or minor as required class (equivalent to CRW 3013).In this honors-level introductory course students will practice writing, reading, and responding to works of poetry, fiction, and creative nonfiction. Organized in three five-week units, students will begin working with the smallest possible unit of output in the given genre (six-word stories, for instance, in fiction) and ending reading a book-length work. Students will submit works of poetry, fiction, and creative nonfiction for both small-group peer review and full-class discussion. By the end of the course, students will have learned and applied critical vocabulary in all three genres, written responses to their own and their peers' work, and prepared themselves for genre-specific creative-writing courses.

This course introduces students to the practice of writing creatively across three literary genres: fiction, nonfiction, and poetry. Together, we will study the craft elements that shape each genre, examining published works as models and inspiration. Students will draft and revise original pieces in all three forms, sharing their work in workshop for constructive feedback.

This class is designed to introduce foundational elements of craft through critical reading, thoughtful critique and discussion of peer writing, and practice. Together, we will explore several essential creative concepts across three units: fiction, poetry, and creative nonfiction.
In this entry-level course,
students read literary texts to develop an understanding of authorial decisions
in contemporary writing in poetry, fiction, and literary nonfiction. Students
will increase their knowledge of relevant writing terminology and concepts and
gain insight into the emphases and specialties of the UCF creative writing
program. Students will also become familiar with professional pathways
including publishing and other applications of a degree in English with a
specialization in creative writing. By mapping a plan for ongoing writing
practice, students will also identify possible avenues to pursue writing

In this entry-level course, students will read literary texts to feed their understanding of authorial decisions in contemporary writing in fiction, literary nonfiction, scriptwriting, and poetry. Students will become fluent in relevant writing terminology and concepts, gain insight into the emphases and specialties of the UCF creative writing program, identify possible career paths and “uses” of a degree in English with a specialization in creative writing; and familiarize themselves with the publishing process.

This is a creative writing workshop class that is a "safe-place" to write original fiction work. Students will read published fiction work, write flash fiction practice pieces, develop a publishable short fiction story, hone skills as editors of peer writing within the workshop platform, and discover how the revision process is when, and where, the real writing occurs. To achieve these goals, the class will take part in "Go to Class" assignments where students study published work, create reading responses, then partake in craft-related discussion; each week students will then craft stress-free practice fiction pieces based on craft elements present in the reading for the week. The assignments work well to best facilitate the classroom experience in an online course. Textbook reading and lecture quizzes allow instructor assessment for the student's progression in required course materials. The major work of the semester is a single short work of fiction over the semester. This piece of writing will begin as a rough draft, then developed, workshopped, and polished to create a piece of marketable writing. Students will immerse themselves in the workshop process by creating critiques in ana editorial style, offering useful, constructive feedback for classmates, while receiving critiques on their own drafts.
CRW 3120 is an intermediate level fiction writing workshop for English
majors. Our focus will be on the close reading of contemporary fiction. We will
explore fiction theory and study the short story for its elements: character,
plot, setting, point of view, and more. We will also learn to read, analyze,
and critique our own work and the work of our peers.
An
intermediate level fiction writing workshop for English majors incorporating
small and large group feedback, analysis, and criticism. Students will complete
in-class writing exercises as well as online assignments. Together we will read
and analyze contemporary literary fiction throughout the semester with a focus
on craft to gain an understanding of common techniques and elements of fiction.
In this course, students will gain a deeper understanding of contemporary
fiction through analyzing short stories and participating in workshop. This
course will place equal emphasis on generative writing and close reading. In
the first weeks of the semester, we will work on “scaffolding” exercises,
taking time to review and bolster our knowledge of the basic components of
fiction. The bulk of the course will be workshop, in which students will read
and constructively critique each other’s stories, and discussions of student
presentations based on assigned stories. The semester will culminate in a final
portfolio with a revision statement.
This
course focuses on short fiction. We’ll read, analyze, and discuss published
stories, as well as workshop original stories of our own. Students will prepare
written feedback (workshop notes) for story submissions and engage in rigorous
group discussion. Over the course of the semester, students will write and
submit two original short stories of approximately 2500 words each.
Learning
goals include gaining familiarity with contemporary fiction, learning
techniques to write successful original fiction, and learning how to
constructively analyze and revise drafts of original fiction in terms of
character and storyline, while considering foundational elements of craft such
as effective characterization, point of view, dialogue, and plot.
As
one would expect with a workshop, the course will involve a lot of group
discussion, in which everyone is expected to participate. Solid participation
will require the stories, both published and student-submitted, be read and
considered deeply prior to the class period in which they are up for
discussion. In this way, we can all learn together, with the outcome being we
improve our own stories as well as our editorial acumen.

Stories are so common in our lives that we often take them for granted. In this class, we will slow down and ask some seemingly basic questions about stories and how we make them. What is a story? How does a story work? Why/how does a story move us?

I am calling this class “Eight Beginnings, Three Middles, and an End.” That’s because you will write the beginning of eight story sketches and then expand three of them into “middles,” and finish one complete story (with an end).

Your “beginnings” will be responses to short story readings for the first eight weeks of class. In other words, you will use the readings as occasions to write your own stories. I encourage you to imitate and emulate the authors we read however you see fit. In the final third of the course, you will revise, expand, and develop three of your eight stories.

Along the way, we will focus on nitty-gritty techniques of writing fiction: voice, style, mood, character, point of view, dialogue, tension, conflict, style, setting and—of course—beginnings, middles, and endings.
While we will mostly be reading short stories in this class, we will also read one play and one novel to help us think more broadly about storytelling techniques and plot devices.

I value emotional and formal risk-taking. I value hard work. I value openness to criticism and a sense of humor, especially about yourself. Respect for others. Community building. Empathy for all your characters. Complex details and themes. Specificity in language. A sense of place. Surprise. Above all, passion for reading and writing and paying attention to being alive.

This course is for students interested in turning lived experience into compelling writing. We’ll read contemporary essays and experiment with scene, voice, image, reflection, structure, and research, then try those techniques in two longer essays. The class includes frequent writing exercises, peer workshop, and a final portfolio of revised creative nonfiction.
This is a compressed online course at the introductory/intermediate
level that will explore contemporary techniques in poetry through reading and
writing. Students will complete weekly discussions, reading responses, poetry
writing exercises, and peer critique, finishing the semester with a portfolio
of original poems.
The best poetry is one which engages in a
dialogue with poets from across the world, and from across periods; and with
the poets of the past and those exercising and sharpening their craft in the
contemporary moment. The best works of poetry are inspired and nurtured by
reading and listening to other poets, and even other writers in general, and
discovering the nuances of language that can affect your poetry in a deep and
intimate way. We will write poetry this semester by engaging with poets – both
from the past, and of the present; poetry from across the world, as well as
poetry written by American pets; including contemporary American poets.
In this course, our objective would be discovery, exploration, and
expression/production of original poetry. There will be four units of class this semester. Each
unit will contain modules for three weeks of activity. The first week in each
unit will be devoted to experiencing, exploring, and discussing modern and
contemporary poetry. The second week in the unit will be devoted to writing
poetry; and the third week will be workshop with your peers that would help you
develop your voice and other technical aspects of the craft of poetry through
close reading. You will be encouraged, as well as required to experiment with
various styles and techniques, and to develop confidence and originality, as
well as expand your range of language and imagery that should enrich your
experience; your power of expression, as well as your ability to contribute to
poetic discourse.

This course is for students who want to read, write, and experiment with contemporary poetry. We’ll study how poets use image, sound, line, form, voice, and other elements of craft, then try those techniques in our own work. The class is highly generative and includes writing exercises, peer workshop, and a final portfolio of revised original poems. No particular style—or prior identity as a “poet”—is required.

This course is an Online course. This means that we shall have our class conducted online. We will read from a variety of poetry from across the world, that reflects the plurality of the poetic experience and its many traditions. We shall read these poems closely, examine their formal structure, and identify textual variety in poetry. The course is not designed as a historical survey but as a general, exploratory discussion on the art and craft of poetry. Its approach is to engage and examine poetry from various directions – as a shapely product of the imagination; as a form of distinct utterance - public and private, as highly stylized and aesthetically arranged exploration into unique psychological worlds, and as a product of a social moment. Generally, poetry offers intellectual stimulation, linguistic pleasures, as well as moral insights. It presents, as well, its own unique aesthetic and interpretive difficulties, perhaps because it radiates between two zones of reality - our private lives as readers, and our public lives as writers. Students will engage in extensive discussions about the making of poems as well as understand the elements that make poetic production possible: that is the aesthetic, social, cultural, historical and political conditions to which the poetic imagination responds. We will analyze poetry from the 20th-century poetry to now. The course attempts to take into broad account the traditional elements of poetry and their contemporary alternatives. There will be weekly writing assignments, including some exercises in poetic craft.
The purpose of the course is to learn
about film screenplay structure, analyze writing strategies and plot
progression in short films, learn and apply correct script form, and creatively
engage in the various stages of original scriptwriting.
The assignments will include technical
writing skills required in scriptwriting, proper structure of action and

analyzing dramatic structure and visualizing dramatic elements as that is what
makes for good movies.
By using the assigned book and online
resources, you will read, watch, and complete written exercises designed to aid
you in the completion of your own original script.

This Integrative-Learning Experience (IE) course will introduce students to the basic theories and practices associated with game design, including brainstorming, the elements of gameplay, artificial intelligence, and storytelling within dynamic, interactive systems. Articles written by experts in the field will be analyzed as we explore the challenges and pitfalls of attempting to merge narratives with games. Students will conceive and outline their own game and produce interactive scripts for elements such as cut scenes and scripted events to be workshopped in class. Each student will produce a 30–40-page Game Design Document (GDD) for an original game with an emphasis on narrative design (since this is a writing course). Student learning outcomes include being able to analyze theories of game design and recognize how they influence narratives within games; justify effective writing techniques for developing original video games; solve design issues such as creating player agency and addressing linearity in story development; manage the design phase of a game by creating a goal-based writing schedule to achieve each milestone; refine and adapt game pitches for peers, the instructor, and industry professionals beyond UCF; compile game design documents that demonstrates mastery of course content; and reflect on design work and how it might be used in game development communities around the globe.

Participating within The
Cypress Dome requires at least two in-person semesters (fall 2026 and
spring 2027) at UCF. Please visit our website to apply. Applications are due
March 15th and require a resume and a reference from a UCF instructor. If you
have any questions or encounter any issues, contact the director, Professor
Kianna Greene (kianna.greene@ucf.edu).
The
Cypress Dome is UCF’s
undergraduate literary journal run for students and by students, published
annually by The Cypress Dome Society. Established in 1989, The Cypress
Dome’s primary objective has been elevating student voices through the
publication of poetry, fiction, creative nonfiction, and visual art. Every part
of the process from reading submissions, copyediting, designing, producing, and
promoting the journal is done by a group of twenty students in a two-semester
long commitment. Students of any major or skillset are encouraged to apply, as The
Cypress Dome gives experience in editing, graphic design, advertising,
promotions, and more!

This class offers intensive practice in reading and writing short fiction, including peer feedback. We’ll read and study published pieces of short fiction, learn about and apply craft techniques, all while building and revising a single piece of fiction over the course of the term.
Note that you must have a copy of the textbook, Deepening Fiction: A Practical Guide for Intermediate and Advanced Writers by Sarah Stone and Ron Nyren, by the first day of the term.
In
this expedited summer course, students will undertake an advanced study and
practice of writing the short story. Students will develop skills in close
reading, craft analysis, generative writing, revision, and peer review,
building upon concepts from CRW 3120. At the end of the course, students will
have a more informed sense of craft techniques required for evocative and
engaging literary fiction; better understand their inspirations, processes, and
needs for successful artistic output; connect with a community of fellow
writers with whom to collaborate; and strategize future plans for writing and
revising.

In this workshop course you will write a 3000-4,000-word short story and read those written by our peers. We will get to know each other, share our love of literature, and trade story ideas before we begin reading and critiquing each other's work in earnest. You will be expected to participate in this discussion in three ways: as readers you will be expected to read, consider, and discuss a wide range of contemporary stories; as writers you will be expected to produce one complete full-length, fully revised short story which will be discussed in workshop; and as peer editors you will be expected to produce thoughtful critiques (400 words minimum) of all work put forward in workshop (as many as fifteen or more comprehensive critiques) and to actively participate in discussion. Student learning outcomes include Scene vs. Summary; Point of View (Perspective, Omniscience, Narrative Distance; Character & Interiority (Complexity, Desires vs. Obstacles); Dialogue & Voice (including Formatting); Setting (Concrete Imagery, Sensory Details, Viewpoint & Perception); Plot & Structure (Tense, Acute vs. Chronic Tension/Top vs. Bottom story, Pacing).

We’ll read, analyze, and discuss published stories, as well as workshop

Learning goals include gaining
familiarity with contemporary fiction, learning techniques to write successful
original fiction, and learning how to constructively analyze and revise drafts
of original fiction in terms of character, structure, and language, while
considering foundational elements of literary craft such as effective
characterization, story shape, point of view, dialogue, and sentence-level
language choices.
As one would expect with a workshop,

expected to participate. Solid participation will require the stories, both
published and student-submitted, be read and considered deeply prior to the
class period in which they are up for discussion. In this way, we can all learn
together, with the outcome being we improve our own stories as well as our
editorial acumen.

How do great writers do what they do? How does a writer create a voice that feels entirely their own? How does a story generate tension, surprise us, move us, or make us see the world differently? And how can we steal some of these tricks for ourselves?

In this class, we will approach the writing of fiction through the art of imitation. We will read closely and widely, studying some of the greatest short story writers, and then try our hands at writing like them. We will borrow their voices, structures, sentences, techniques, and ways of creating . The idea is not to become a second-rate version of another writer, but to discover new possibilities for our own work by attempting things we might never have thought to do on our own.

Each week, we will read stories by writers with distinctive approaches to fiction and use those stories as models for our own experiments. We will pay close attention not only to what these writers do, but how they do it: how they handle time, build characters, construct scenes, manipulate point of view, create tension, and make their sentences move. We will think about what a story tells us and what it leaves unsaid, what its form makes possible, and what we can learn by taking it apart and putting it back together.

Along the way, you will write a series of imitations and experiments, some of which you will develop into longer, more fully realized stories. Because this is an advanced fiction course, we will spend considerable time thinking about revision, not simply as a process of fixing what doesn't work, but as a way of discovering what a story might become.

What makes a world? What strategies can we use as writers to craft worlds that are immersive, “lived-in,” and compelling? In this course, we’ll ask a lot of questions about our world as well as the worlds we build on the page. We’ll read a mixture of fiction, essays, theory, and poetry. This course will likely include a trip to the university archives. You can expect a lot of in-class writing and sharing; this is a generative class and may include a workshop unit. Over the course of the semester, we will build a world as a class and write a full-length project in it. A large amount of collaboration and collaborative writing is required for this course. Anyone who takes this course should be prepared to regularly contribute to our collaborative world-building project. Your final project will be either a portfolio of original creative work or instructor-approved self-designed project.
This is a workshop-based course in literary nonfiction (memoir,
personal essay, and—in some semesters—literary journalism). We’ll focus on
craft-based discussions of new student writing and studies of selected
published works as a way of informing our understanding of craft. Students will
write sketches, full manuscripts, and craft studies. Reading is expected to
include: The Boys of My Youth, by Jo Ann Beard; The Best American Essays 2013,

This Writing Workshop is an intensive
creative writing clinic for honing the craft of poetry. It will involve both
Critique and Writing. Students are expected to take charge of this workshop by
providing clear feedback to their peers, through the writing process
underscored by three key principles and outcomes of this workshop. The
principles of craft, analysis and rigor. Rigor means the care you put into the
craft, and it demands self-criticism and personal aesthetic accountability.
Analysis presupposes an acquisition of critical insight that will help you in
the long run examine carefully and engage in the meaningful discussion of
poetry and poetics, with insight and clarity. You will engage in a critique of
your peers mindful of your awareness of the craft of poetry, with respect and
empathy, as well as with honesty. As a community, we will be accountable to
each other; we will engage in meaningful and respectful discussions, first of
the general principles and constraints of craft using the examples of our class
readings, then with each other's work. In other words, we will read established
poets, and using their examples, craft and revise our own poems through a
workshop process. We will consider how well we arrange language, and structure
the topography of the poem with care and intention. We will workshop our poems,
revise, and submit our works, within the very constraints of allowable time
this summer. By the end of this workshop, each student would have written and
revised a set of 5 poems in different forms, around the subject of Space, the
found Object, the Magic of Night and waking, and on Music. These themes shall
form the larger subjects of our detailed and unique responses.

This advanced poetry-writing workshop asks students to exercise and stretch their poetic strengths through writing in metrical and free-verse forms, reading full-length collections by acclaimed contemporary poets, and responding to each other's work with genre-specific vocabulary on a regular basis. The course will be divided into craft elements (imagery, address, figure, syntax, meter, rhyme, etc.) with weekly poetic prompts focused on each element. Students will also research, read, and write about living poets of their choosing in order to expand and hone their poetic affinities. By the end of the course, students will have revised and curated a portfolio of poems suitable for inclusion in a graduate creative-writing admissions packet or an application for a writer's conference.
In this fully online course, students
will write approximately twenty pages of screenplay material, along with
committed critiques of their peers' work. A wide range of projects will be
considered, including but not limited to short films, feature films, one-hour
episodic television scripts, half-hour comedy scripts, and scripts for animated
series. Students should come well-prepared to discuss the course materials, the
work of their peers, and have a STRONG knowledge of screenplay format, since
CRW 3610 (the intro course) is a prerequisite here. We will assume you have
mastered format. If you have not, review screenplay format before taking this
class. You have been warned! At the end of the semester, students will submit
their very best (and often heavily revised pages) along with a revision
reflection that details this process. Ultimately, we want to see your script
actually produced, so we’ll always be writing with an aim toward production.

This course helps prepare you, a student in a technical profession or professional field, for the types of research, writing, and information presentation that you will encounter in your career after graduation. Writing has many purposes and uses beyond just relaying information, and even in the most concrete of professions, the facts do not “speak for themselves.” Your task as a writer is to articulate, explain, and interpret the information you are dealing with. Throughout your career, you will need to understand the social context of your writing and its audiences, and you will need to master the techniques of crafting your writing to suit your purposes and the interests of your audience. This course covers important professional writing genres, including resumes, proposals, presentations, and research reports.

Students will critically evaluate video games as rhetorical devices and will learn techniques for dealing with particular game design strategies such as artificial intelligence, storytelling, cueing, and establishing/maintaining immersion. In order to better understand game literacies, students will be expected to produce a group-produced game design document (GDD). In this course, we will address
"wicked problems," which include problems affecting the environment
(the 6th extinction, depletion of natural resources, climate change), human
society (authoritarianism, propaganda, cults), public health (pollution, guns,
addiction, vaccine hesitancy), civil rights (degradation of voting rights,
reproduction rights, immigrant rights), and the economy (growing inequality,
market volatility, externalities). They are resistant to resolution because of
"incomplete or contradictory knowledge, the number of people and opinions
involved, the large economic burden, and the interconnected nature of these
problems with other problems" (AC4D). What can we do? We will turn to
theory and methodology.
Digital Rhetoric and the Modern Dialectic takes a humanities-based approach, exploring how
rhetoric, dialectic, critical theory, art, media, and digital practices shape
our understanding of technology, society, and ourselves. Rather than simply
studying existing digital rhetoric, students will invent new rhetorical and
dialectical practices for digital media, with a major focus on creating a
“widesite”—a personalized digital tool for addressing the most pressing problems of our age. Drawing on Gregory Ulmer’s
concept of “electracy,” the course examines modernist and postmodernist
approaches across literature, visual art, film, music, and essays while
encouraging students to experiment with style and develop new forms of writing
and communication.
Title: Qualitative User Research for Real-World Impact.

Course Description: Teaches students how to conduct rigorous qualitative research (such as interviews, focus groups, and observational research) to inform the design of impactful information products, such as public safety trackers, cybersecurity guides, or mobile apps.
Learning Objectives: Collect and code qualitative data and synthesize research findings into actionable design reports and strategic recommendations.

In this course, we will examine the broad field of technical editing and explore how it has changed over time. After developing foundational knowledge about the history and practice of technical editing, we will spend the remainder of the semester learning about editing strategies and the function of technical editing in a range of professions. Students will have opportunities to practice technical editing individually and collaboratively. Major projects will include a special topics presentation, individual copy-editing challenges, and a final team-based substantive technical editing project. Although there are no scheduled class meetings, students in this course are expected to attend a one-on-one conference with the professor as well as 2 Zoom meetings with their team for the final editing project. By the end of the course, you should have multiple samples of your professional editing work to share with potential employers, in a portfolio, or on a professional website.
This course explores the
challenges and opportunities of using AI and augmentation technologies in

AI in TPC work and scholarship. The final project for this class is the
development of a robust corporate AI policy that responds to the ethical and
material concerns of various stakeholders in a specified context.
The Technical Communication of Video Games
In this asynchronous, online course, students will analyze video
games as complex, interactive communication systems that operationalize and
advance core principles of technical communication. The course focuses on how
games structure instruction, feedback, and user guidance through multimodal
interaction, including text, sound, visuals, and embodied input. Students will
apply technical communication research methods such as usability testing,
heuristic evaluation, and user studies to evaluate game design and user/player
experience. These analyses position video games as instructive models for
contemporary technical communication challenges, including interactive
documentation, AI‑mediated communication, and accessibility‑driven interface
design.
This
course investigates how key concepts such as disability, access, universal
design, plain language, and ethics inform the practice of technical
communication. Students consider how policy and technology changes have shaped
disabled people's experiences with technical communication. Assignments
prioritize audience awareness and offer opportunities to apply theory to
practice. In the first eight weeks of the semester, students may be
assigned 75-100 pages of reading per week. Major assignments may include
individual and collaborative primary research projects, technology experiments,
and live or recorded presentations. Some assignments may require the use of
genAI. To succeed in this course, you need access to the MS Office Suite, MS
Teams, and Zoom (available for free to UCF students - https://it.ucf.edu/ucf-apps/),
as well as a device that allows you to run and record audio and video. Please
check UCF Libraries and your local library for copies of the assigned texts
before purchasing them.
This capstone course will support you in creating a digital portfolio, with the overarching goal to

rigorous theoretical framing. Your portfolio will contain a set of artifacts (documents you have
produced) for specific audiences and purposes in alignment with your professional identity and the

Your sense of professional identity as a competent technical communicator will vary depending on
your goals and career trajectory. The capstone experience can help you to synthesize content from
your work throughout the program as you recognize habits of mind, skills, and key theoretical or
methodological approaches that have emerged across your programmatic experiences.
Ultimately, a well-composed portfolio demonstrates a clear sense of professional identity, ability to
reflect upon and illustrate skills, and preparedness to transition to another setting (e.g., the workplace,
the academy, a doctoral program).
Questions you’re invited to explore include:
• How do I develop a portfolio that showcases my rhetorical finesse, design savvy, and academic
acumen?
• Why is theoretical framing important for portfolio development and artifact revision?
• How do I showcase ethical communication competencies and why does it matter in a portfolio?
• What are distinctions between an industry-, teaching-, or research-focused portfolio, and what role
does academic framing play across these genre variations?

paragraphs: As a required course for the major, “Theories of
Literature” is designed to introduce students to the theory and practice of
contemporary approaches to the scholarly study of literary and cultural texts.
The course covers many of the most prominent and influential “schools of
thought” or critical theories of literature over the past century, including
New Criticism, structuralism, poststructuralism/deconstruction, psychoanalysis,
feminism, sexuality/queer studies, Marxism, new historicism, postcolonial theory,
race and ethnic studies, reader response, disability studies, and
eco-criticism. We will study explanatory texts about the various theories,
along with representative texts of theory itself. We will also apply these
approaches to literary and cultural texts ranging from canonical works to
popular forms (such as film). We will engage with the current scholarly debate
in literary studies and work toward the construction of an advanced analytical
paper in preparation for 4000-level coursework.
This class will
introduce you to various theories of literature, from New Criticism to
Psychoanalysis, to Marxism and Gender Studies. We will be doing a lot of reading in this short,
six-week semester from Robert Dale Parker’s How to Interpret Literature. We will cover approximately two
theories per week, and apply them to short stories and poems.
Theories
of Literature will introduce you to ways of accessing texts that will open them
up to more varied and challenging readings. Although the critical and
theoretical approaches we will study are often complex and daunting, by the end
of the semester you will be able to recognize and apply the approaches to a
variety of literary and cultural texts. The theoretical background and writing
skills you acquire should increase your understanding of literature,
authorship, and literary analysis. Questioning the assumptions behind our ways
of reading and meaning making is an activity we engage in often, and as a
result, we will have dynamic class discussions that leave nothing uncontested.
We will work hard not to stereotype or marginalize critical or theoretical
approaches that seem "strange" or "old-fashioned" to us.

designed to provide students with a vocabulary and a context for their own work

learn how to apply these theoretical key terms to a variety of different

reduced seat time and an online component. Students will be expected to
complete all reading assignments, to participate regularly and productively
online and face-to-face discussions and assignments, to conduct independent
research, and to write theoretically informed textual analyses.

"A political view of textual scholarship locates editorial practice and theory within the broadest conceptions of literary and cultural study." Michelle R. Warren, The Politics of Textual Scholarship.

ENG 4832 teaches the skills that careers in publishing actually require, proofreading, copyediting, style-guide fluency (Chicago, MLA, APA), scholarly-journal production, and digital editing, and it treats those skills as something more than mechanical. The course's guiding idea is that editing is never neutral. Every editorial decision, from choosing a copy-text to enforcing a house style to selecting a publishing platform, is an exercise of power over meaning. It decides whose voice counts as "correct," what enters the archive, and what a text is allowed to say. You will graduate with a portfolio of genuine, marketable editorial skills and the critical self-awareness that separates an editor from a spell-checker. Across the semester we follow the field's central argument, between the intentionalist tradition (the editor recovers the author's intention) and the social-text tradition (the text is a collaborative, material object made by many hands). This course is a core requirement for the UCF Editing and Publishing Undergraduate Certificate.

the general aim of introducing you to a range of research methods and related
professional issues in the field of English, this course has several goals.

ways, for example, that cultural studies enable us to engage texts from

technical communication. Third, in addition to examining specific

scholarship. The course concludes with a collaborative digital humanities
assignment using textual encoding and an examination of career paths.

earliest and greatest writers of the English language, from the medieval period
through the late eighteenth-century. We will investigate authors and texts from

The successful student will demonstrate a thorough understanding of the
readings through weekly assignments that require both critical thinking and

This
course offers a broad survey of authors, texts, and genres from the medieval
period through the late eighteenth century, covering approximately 1000 years
of English literature. As a survey, this class presents particular challenges,
as we seek to cover a breadth of material without sacrificing depth of
understanding. A wide base of knowledge, effective communication skills, and

in college and beyond, and practicing these vitally important skills lays the

will learn and explore different methods of analyzing and criticizing a

In this

"Did Women Have a
Renaissance?" (J. Kelly-Gadol). Renaissance women were often
stereotypically portrayed—or objectified—as silent, chaste, pious, and
obedient. Faced with many challenges, if not outright barriers, they struggled
in their pursuit of knowledge and basic artistic literacy. This course, through
selected texts, seeks to explore two key aspects: first, how Renaissance women
were portrayed by the male writing class, and second, how some women of the
period actively and vocally engaged in writing and publishing to re-fashion,
interpret, and comment on the world around them. The course offers an
innovative, interdisciplinary analysis of Renaissance women writers, while also
providing an overview of current feminist approaches. It argues for the
critical importance of reconsidering Renaissance writers in today’s context,
inviting reflection on what these historical voices have to offer now and, in
the future, and how our past continues to inform the present, and vice versa.
Focusing on literature by and about women in the Renaissance, the course is
structured into biweekly modules, each featuring a single author and their
primary text(s). These readings are supported by two scholarly articles per
module, each offering unique perspectives on the text and its themes. By
synthesizing these articles in their analysis of the primary readings, students
engage with critical scholarship, practice analytical skills, and participate
in the broader scholarly conversation surrounding both Early Modern Women’s
literature and contemporary feminist theory.
This course is a historical survey of British Literature
during the Restoration Era (1660-1700). In this course you will be introduced
to major Restoration thinkers, including John Milton, the Earl of Rochester and
Aphra Behn. You will be tasked to think historically about Restoration
literature in order to generate focused and convincing analytical arguments
based on close reading of literary and non-literary texts (i.e. recognizing,
understanding, and explaining a text's formal and content-based elements).
A study of Gothic
literature (prose, poetry, drama) in the British Isles and its cultural
contexts. We will map out the trajectory of black presence in British
Literature using the lenses of history, politics, and culture. We will observe
Britain’s painful process of naming/ renaming of the black presence, and the

When we think of the
Victorians, we often picture earnest social reformers tugging at our
heartstrings in novels about orphans (Charles Dickens’s Oliver Twist) or
meticulous realists offering a detailed account of the day-to-day lives of
ordinary people (George Eliot’s Middlemarch), but the latter decades of the
nineteenth century saw the rise of a counterculture in Victorian England that
espoused, instead, “art for art’s sake,” embracing artifice, ornament, and
playful excess. Members of the so-called Aesthetic Movement, and its outgrowth,
the Decadent Movement, advocated for pleasure in beauty, rejecting art’s moral
and representational obligations. At the same time, they challenged traditional
gender roles and cultural norms. In this course we’ll explore poetry, fiction,
and nonfiction by British authors who broke new ground aesthetically and
socially in the 1870s–90s, such as: Walter Pater, Algernon Charles Swinburne,
Oscar Wilde, Vernon Lee, Arthur Machen, Sarojini Naidu, and Amy Levy. Alongside
the literary works, we will explore visual arts by important Aesthetes and
Decadents, including James Abbott McNeill Whistler, Aubrey Beardsley, and
Simeon Solomon.
ENL 3451 is a 3000
level course with its focus on various issues and themes of British literature
from the late eighteenth to the long nineteenth century. The overarching theme
of this course varies from semester to semester. This semester, the course
will present a historical overview of British literature during the long
nineteenth century with special emphasis on the emergence of science fiction.
The list of authors will include Mary Shelley, Jane Loudon, and H.G. Wells,
among a few others.
"Tolkien’s Bookshelf".

As Gandalf, Aragorn, Gimli, and Legolas approach Théoden’s hall in Rohan, Aragon begins to chant in a language unknown to the elf and dwarf and, as Legolas guesses it to be the language of the Rohirrim, the future king offers a translation: “Where now the horse and the rider? Where is the horn that was blowing? / Where is the helm and the hauberk, and the bright hair flowing? / Where is the hand on the harpstring, and the red fire glowing? / Where is the spring and the harvest and the tall corn growing?” As any good bit of worldbuilding, this poetic digression gives the audience some sense of the people of Rohan and their culture. It also tells us a bit about Tolkien the author. Tolkien’s day job was as a professor of medieval English literature at Oxford, and one of the early medieval poems he undoubtedly studied was one now called The Wanderer, which has a familiar ring to its middle section: “What has become of the horse? What has become of the warrior? What has become of the treasure-giver? / What has become of the banquet-seats? Where are the hall-revelries?” As is evident in this example, Tolkien developed a deep knowledge of early English and other literatures produced by the cultures of northwestern Europe, which influenced his work as a fantasy author. In this course, we will read translations of the works (mostly medieval) that inspired Tolkien: Old English poems, Norse mythology and poetry, and Finnish epic, among others. Though the focus of this class will largely be on the works that inspired Tolkien rather than his work, we will read some of his poetry, shorter fiction, as well as sections from The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.

In her 1919 essay “Modern Fiction” Virginia Woolf complained that real life could not be captured by conventional fiction: “if a writer were a free man … if he could write what he chose, not what he must, if he could base his work upon his own feeling and not upon convention, there would be no plot, no comedy, no tragedy, no love interest or catastrophe in the accepted style.” This course will examine the impetus in Modernism to generate new aesthetic modes, beyond “the accepted style” of previous generations, in order to represent the often-cataclysmic social changes in the first half of the twentieth century. We will explore how works of literature challenge conventional expectations as they experiment with form and content and as they grapple with problems of changing gender roles, of the devastation of WWI, and of the legacies of colonialism and racism at the end of the British Empire. This course is a W course, which means that it is entirely online. Students must have reliable access to a computer and Internet. Students will be expected to complete all reading assignments, to participate regularly and productively in online individual and group assignments, to conduct independent research, and to write literary analyses.

course will explore three iconic women novelists of early 18th century, who
have become an inevitable part of England’s literary history. To be specific,
the focus of this course will be on the Brontë sisters. We will read novels and

novels: Northanger Abbey, Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice,

We will read a novel and one or two articles every two weeks. There will be

various moral, political, and aesthetic issues raised in his plays and poetry.

Shakespeare’s works to Renaissance-era visual art and cinema. Additionally, we

enduring relevance in today’s world. Plays will be supplemented by readings in
Shakespearean criticism and contemporary theory. The course is structured into
weekly modules, each dedicated to a single author and primary text(s). These
primary readings will be supported by two scholarly articles per module, each
offering unique perspectives. Through synthesis and analysis of these sources,
students will engage with critical scholarship and contribute to broader
discussions in Early Modern literature and contemporary theory. By undertaking
close readings of Shakespeare’s texts, alongside visual artifacts such as
Renaissance paintings, this course will provide insight into Early Modern
culture and explore broader themes of cultural identity, nationhood, and
individuality.

Who’s
afraid of John Milton? In posing this question, the course aims to analyze
Milton’s powerful and decisive influence and impact on the English literary
Canon. This course focuses on John Milton’s lyric and epic poetry, prose, and
letters, with a particular emphasis on his biblical epic, Paradise Lost.
Published in 1667, Milton’s poem tells the story of Adam and Eve’s
disobedience, their exile from Eden, and Satan’s war against God himself.
Written in the aftermath of the English Civil War, Paradise Lost is an epic
that explores the themes of free will, gender, obedience and defiance,
republicanism, and the nature of good and evil. The seminar aims to facilitate
a close reading of Milton’s poem and its themes, while introducing seminal
critical interpretations and current critical/theoretical debates.
Undertaking
close readings of specific Milton’s texts as well as visual artefacts such as
engravings and paintings, the course provides a unique insight into Milton and
Early Modern’s culture and helps refashion, re-map broader issues that engage
the then emergent status of cultural and religious identity, nation, and
individuality. Finally, the course argues for the critical importance of
thinking Milton now. We will therefore consider what Milton has to offer now
(in an age of global cultures) and in the future.
Do you use
"friend" as a verb? Why do some people say "aks" and not
"ask"? How many different ways can you use the word like? When does
“I’m busy” mean “no”? In this course, we will study the English language and
how it works. We will connect technical linguistic information to your daily
experiences with language. We will learn and practice techniques for describing
English, both its words and sentences and larger elements of discourse in
context. In linguistic terms, we’ll cover phonology, morphology, semantics,
pragmatics, speech act theory, and language variation.
Beowulf, the
oldest narrative poem in the English language, begins: Hwæt! We Gar-Dena in
geardagum þeodcyninga þrym gefrunon, hu þa æþelingas ellen fremedon.
There’s not much here that looks anything close to the language we speak today.
How can this be called English!? But, upon closer inspection, there are certain
recognizable words: weremains unchanged in Modern English as a plural
pronoun; hwæt, though it uses a strange letter in the middle, becomes
“what,” as spelling conventions switched around the “h” and “w”; the “g” in gear was
pronounced with a “y”-sound, and when spelling caught up with pronunciation,
became “year.” Though these lines look like a completely different
language, there are hints of the English we speak today even within this
excerpt. How did the English of Beowulf become the language that we
use daily? How did its sounds, spellings, syntax, and vocabulary change so
drastically over time? These are the key questions of this course, which
introduces students to basic linguistic concepts while we explore the constantly
changing English language from its earliest forms, stretching back around
fourteen hundred years ago, to its variations and dialects spoken in the
present. As we journey through this long history together, we’ll consider
topics such as: why does Old English look like a foreign language? What are
English’s closest linguistic relatives? How did contact with other languages
and cultures shape English throughout its history? Is English more difficult
than other languages? Why do people always complain about English spelling?
Where does the idea of “proper” English come from?
As with any language, English is constantly
changing, and attention to the circumstances that brought about its changes can
alert us to the ways that English may shift in the future. Our course will
trace the historical route of English as it developed from a tongue spoken in
only a small corner of the North Atlantic to the most widely spoken language in
the world by means of readings from This Language, A River (Smith
and Kim), in addition to a few supplementary readings posted as pdfs on the
course website. Several assessments punctuate the course throughout the
semester including semi-regular tests and problem sets, a midterm and final, as
well as two projects (the expectations for which will be clearly communicated
beforehand!). By the end of the course, you will understand where English came
from, where it is presently, and where it might go, in addition to having a
broader understanding of language change and the relationship between language
and culture.

Can you explain the difference between transitive and
intransitive verbs? Between complements and objects? Between clauses and
phrases? Between active and passive voice? This grammar class will teach you
how. English grammar is a fascinating subject that transcends questions such
as, "Is it ok to end a sentence with a preposition?" Even the simple
rules are not as simple as you might think. Experts often disagree, for
example, about where to put the comma. Unfortunately, many self-appointed grammar
cops know little about how the English language actually works. It is true that
if you're a native speaker of English, you're already an expert. However, this
expertise is "innate"--it isn't conscious knowledge, but subconscious
knowledge. In this class, you'll learn to consciously understand how your
language works so you can enhance your own communication skills. Making the
transition from subconscious to conscious knowledge may not be easy. For one
thing, whatever conscious knowledge you already have may be clouded by
inaccuracies, even folklore. Since this class is based on research about how
good speakers and writers actually use English, you may find it difficult
because it’s not what you're used to. For another, making the transition to
conscious knowledge will require frequent practice. Because of this, you'll be
expected to complete several assignments every week, and you'll be encouraged
to complete additional practice exercises on your own. Please note: Writers
benefit from studying grammar in the same way that athletes benefit from
studying anatomy. Grammar isn't a "how to write" class any more than
anatomy is a "how to play your sport" class, but knowing how English
works can help you write more effectively. Because this course covers a vast
amount of material, you should expect to complete dense reading assignments,
numerous homework assignments, and challenging exams. Prerequisites: A grade of
‘C’ (2.0) or better in ENC 1102 and sophomore standing.

LIT 3212 is designated as a
Research-Intensive (RI) course. This designation will be noted on your
transcripts. Your active engagement in the research and/or creative scholarship
process will be the core of your learning experience in this course. A significant
portion of your grade for LIT 3212 will be derived from both your active
participation in the research process and the tangible course-related
project(s) that comes out of said project. If you have any questions about this

Detailed Description: This
course walks you through the process of conducting literary research while
helping to refine your library skills. Along the way, we will draw from the
Association of College and Research Libraries (ACRL) Information Literacy Framework.
According to the ACRL, “Research is iterative and depends upon asking
increasingly complex or new questions whose answers lead to additional
questions or lines of inquiry in any field.” We will discuss this concept more
in-depth throughout the course. Your goal in the course is to produce a
research paper suitable for publication in a literary studies journal.
The course will also focus on
a research project created by Jada, an English major who conducted a literary
study of James Baldwin’s classic short story, “Sonny’s Blues.”
The basic textbook we will be
using for our class is Strategies for Conducting Literary Research, 2e, an Open
Educational Resource (meaning it’s free!). It has loads of concepts and
vocabulary, some of which you may not have encountered before. In a research-based
course, your instructor may require you to write a research paper of 6-12
pages, but the knowledge you need to perform this task can fill up dozens or
hundreds of pages. Writing about literature is a complicated, often messy
process; it needs to meet high standards while incorporating knowledge from
other fields such as psychology, history, science, and other arts. It entails
knowledge about language, genre, structures, styles, and more. To produce good
research about literature, we need to know a lot of things about a lot of
things!

This class offers a historical overview of the genre of SF from the end of the nineteenth century to the contemporary period. We will cover the birth of the genre in the 1890s, the pulp magazine era, the Golden Age of the 40s-50s, the New Wave revolution of the 60-70s, the Cyberpunk movement of the 80s, and end with a smattering of some of the various styles that characterize SF in the past few decades including Afrofuturism, New British Space Opera, and literary sf. Our overall concern throughout the class will be twofold: first, to stress that SF is a genre with a history and that most individual works of SF can only be adequately interpreted in response to that history, and second, to work against the tendency to see science fiction as an essentially escapist genre by striving to connect our novels and stories to their historical, cultural, and political contexts.

According to the National Council for Behavioral Health, “70% of adults in the U.S. have experienced some type of traumatic event at least once in their lives.” While a stubborn stigma remains attached to the public debate on mental health, such a debate has nonetheless increasingly recognized that trauma has become a common feature of contemporary life, leading some observers to claim that we live in an “age of trauma.” Indeed, everyday depictions of trauma populate the cultural landscape, afflicting such fictionalized characters as Katniss Everdeen in The Hunger Games sequels, Tony Stark in Iron Man 3, and Wanda Maximoff of Marvel’s Disney+ series, WandaVision. This new undergraduate course in the Department of English will join the burgeoning field of what’s become known as trauma studies in the humanities by taking up the representation of trauma in a wide range of literary and cultural texts. Although we will draw on scholarship conversant with the medical humanities, for the most part our attention will be given to the ways by which trauma, variously conceived and rendered in narrative form, appears in literary works (novels, short stories, and poems), along with a few films (fiction, documentary, and animated).

This course focuses on literary and creative works from
different genres and international authors addressing issues and stories
related to environmental justice themes, such as toxics and land use. This
semester, we will examine literary representations of environmental justice
from interdisciplinary and cross-cultural perspectives. Instead of focusing on
post-apocalyptic fiction, we will read texts that portray environmental change
as mundane. We will trace the patterns, and possible solutions, that emerge
when we apply environmental humanities methods to complex ecological issues
like sustainability, environmental justice, climate change, energy, and water,

Ultimately, through critical and creative modes of enquiry, we will strive to
understand how artistic and creative expression might enable us to imagine more
equitable futures. We will look at a variety of media and genres, which writers
and artists have utilized to criticize the present and imagine alternative
futures: fiction, poetry, environmental essays and film.

This course will explore the complex relation between literature and war in the 20th Century by pursuing a set of questions for which there are no easy answers: To what extent has literature been responsible for mythologizing war and thus reproducing the very desire that makes militarism alluring? Is literature capable of conveying what war is like through a conventional aesthetic of realism or are other literary modes better equipped to represent such brutal reality? Is there a limit to the capacity of literature to document the horrors of war, horrors that are otherwise unspeakable? Is literature tasked by society with an obligation to act as the conscience of a nation, a form of ethical reflection on the causes and consequences of war? While the course will mostly focus on more traditional forms of literature (poetry, fiction, memoir), we will also make use of recent developments in literary theory that have expanded the notion of a “text,” allowing us to include a wider range of cultural forms (graphic novel, documentary and fiction film, online sources).
In this “a-typical” literature
course, as a class, students are asked to consider the nature of creativity, great
literary writers of the 18th century through the 20th
centuries, and correlations between “the creative mind” and mental illness. The
overarching question asked within the course is, “Where does this thing called
"[creative] madness" (or melancholy, mania, moroseness) in
association with "genius" creativity come from, and at what cost?”
Students examine the creative minds of
historical literary writers through their writings (both private letters and
published works), and our core text, Touched With Fire (Dr. Kay Redfield
Jamison) to consider the mystique, stereotypes, and artistic temperament in
association with creativity and “creative genius." In addition, we will
read Byron’s Poetry and Prose (a Norton Critical Edition) during
full semesters along with Daniel Quinn’s Ishmael. Summer sections will
read Ishmael, and examine selected readings from the Byron text.
Objectives: Through
engagement with the required texts, Go to Class assignments, discussions, and
academic writing, students are encouraged to produce original thinking in the
form of scholarly writing and activities. We explore questions about literary
writers in attempt to come to a deeper understanding of the creative mind,
mental illness, writing methods, and (perhaps most importantly) to experience
these writers not as just “historical figures” but as individual human beings. Students
will then consider how 21st century student writers and scholars of
literature see themselves as writers/authors in relation to historical
depictions of literary writers. This endeavor is accomplished through
thought-provoking exercises, assignments, and discussion.
After completing this
course, students will have an increased ability and knowledge allowing
identification of misrepresentations of authors due to bias, foundational
knowledge of mental health in association with well-known writers and poets, gain
confidence in forming informed opinions, gain experience in using
inter-disciplinary methods as fuel for original thinking, the ability to
perform academic research to high standards, critically analyze sources as well

examine literary works for evidence of "authorial self" or
author-bias within the writing. The work of the course includes analytical
writing, class content contribution and discussion, and a final paper.

relationship to the modernist movement across the arts. It treats the modernist

This course offers an introduction to Old Norse literature, somewhat
broadly conceived, covering mythological material (stories about Thor, Odin,
and Loki, among others), tales of legendary heroes and cursed swords, and the
sagas of the Icelanders, what might be described as the earliest examples of
historical fiction. We begin with a consideration of the “Viking Age,”
examining sources from England that discussed the early “Viking” attacks while
also considering early Scandinavian culture. From there, we jump into the
mythological material in the Prose Edda and in selections from the Poetic Edda,
before reading a short, legendary saga that draws on the mythology. Then, we
move from stories of gods and legendary heroes to those of the historical
heroes who first settled Iceland as we read some of the most famous sagas of
the Icelanders. As we move through each of these topics, we will consider the
historical and cultural contexts necessary for understanding and appreciating
these myths and legends in order to gain an appreciation for “Viking”
literature.

Students will study a broad range of women’s writing and films investigating
how these writers/directors negotiate questions of postcolonial feminism,
agency, national belonging and resistance. We will study short fiction, novels,
poetry, art and films by South Asian women to understand significant concepts
within postcolonial and gender studies . Some of the questions we will think
through are: How do South Asian women’s writing, and films represent women’s
struggles and resistance in the postcolonial national cultures? How do these texts
reconfigure gendered and subaltern agency from colonial and patriarchal
structures? How does women’s art enable spaces of rethinking identity and
normative power structures of class, caste, national and religious violence?
How has women’s writing in south Asia impacted anticolonial movements? And
finally, how does women’s voices reconfigure claims towards identity and
feminist movements through intersectional frameworks?

What is “romance?” What we’ve meant by the term shifts uneasily: it can be a genre, a term for the novel, any text in “vernacular,” and – principally now – a love story. Neither the term nor the literature that carries its name have remained constant. “Romance” proves remarkably malleable, travelling across the languages of the Mediterranean and North Seas: from the chivalric to the provocative, from poetry to prose. In this class, we will explore “romance” texts, centering on their medieval origins and preoccupations with courtly love, quests, love triangles, and knightly adventures across language and cultural divides, seeing how they influence and build upon each other.

This semester, the “Topics in Popular Fiction” course focuses on
climate change, engaging with literary and cinematic representations from
around the world.
Hurricanes, forest fires, melting glaciers
and sea ice, heat waves, and floods worldwide are increasingly drawing our
attention to the harmful effects of man-made climate change. These cataclysmic
changes in the global climate have captured the attention not only of
scientists and environmentalists but also of novelists, poets, and filmmakers.
A new genre of fiction, cli-fi, has emerged over the last two decades,
rendering the current and future realities of global warming more palpable.
In this class, we will consider questions such
as: how and why does cli-fi matter in the context of climate change? Can cli-fi
help alter our conceptions of the earth and our role in changing it? How are
our identities important to the narratives about the ecological crisis?
How do these texts conceive ways of adapting to new realities of climate change
and imagine alternative futures? We will also analyze the specific formal and
stylistic conventions of the genre of cli-fi and situate these texts within
broader debates and discourses—scientific, philosophical, historical, and
political—about climate change.

This class explores modern drama (since the 19th century)
from cross-disciplinary and cross-cultural perspectives. Theorists of drama
stake claims about the most effective ways for dramatists to effect change in
audiences and in the world. Tragic dramas, from the earliest in ancient Greece
to the most recent, have confronted foolishness, traumatic loss, and the
psychic wounds they produce. Comic dramas create critical distance, enabling
thought that can lead to personal and/or collective action. Modern playwrights
have experimented with the forms and materials of tragedies and comedies and
have created genres such as tragicomedy, which combines elements from tragedy
and comedy. Newer forms of drama include ethnographic, avant-garde, and
performance art, which push the boundaries of drama.
This course presents works of drama and theory from a diverse
group of playwrights and authors. Reading drama is never the same as
experiencing a live performance, yet the texts of the drama deserve our
attention as literature. This course consists of modules, readings,
assignments, discussions, and quizzes aimed at improving our understanding of
drama and the impact drama has had on our world.

Fall 2025 author: Salman Rushdie.
Contemporary fiction's most international
and influential writer, Salman Rushdie, is one of the most controversial
figures in recent literary history. An author of Indian heritage, Rushdie has
garnered countless accolades and prestigious international literary awards, as
well as political opponents, resulting in a fatwa condemning him to death and
the fatal stabbing of the author in August 2022. Drawing on his heritage as a
migrant and multiculturalist, Rushdie is considered “the great chronicler of
the global village”. His fiction is celebrated for its intellectual and
linguistic playfulness, historical understanding, and its engagement with
border crossings, both literal and figurative.
In this course, we will consider questions
such as what makes Salman Rushdie a global author. Is Rushdie a champion of
free speech and multiculturalism, or is he an author feeding the “cosmopolitan
alterity industry” that invests in exoticizing cultural differences?
Situating Rushdie’s work within
socio-political and historical contexts, we will approach his writings from
various theoretical positions, including but not limited to postcolonialism,
nationalism, globalization, identity, religion, multiculturalism, gender,
representation, and popular culture. We will read Rushdie’s seminal fiction,
including Midnight’s Children and The Satanic Verses, as
well as more recent novels, such as Quichotte.
